articles.title_orig: The damage of the Manchester City verdict runs deep. An era of Premier League history is tainted - The Athletic
articles.title_zh: The damage of the Manchester City verdict runs deep. An era of Premier League history is tainted - The Athletic
articles.content_orig:
Published: 13:30 EDT, 25 September 2026 | Updated: 16:40 EDT, 25 September 2026
Nothing will ever be quite the same again in English football. On the last Friday in September 2026, something broke irretrievably in our game. Something was ruined. Something was lost. Please don't laugh too bitterly at this, but this was the day when the last of our innocence slunk away into the corner and stood against the wall, its head bowed.
When the news emerged that Manchester City had been found guilty of the vast majority of the 115 charges relating to breaches of the Premier League 's financial regulations, it plunged the game into a pit of fire and a world of recriminations and repercussions that may redraw much of the recent history of the top flight.
This is our Calciopoli Scandal that rocked Italian football in 2006 and relegated the mighty Juventus to Serie B, this is our equivalent of the bribery and match fixing scandal that defrocked Marseille in 1993, this is our Black Sox Scandal that surrounded the fixing of the 1919 World Series. It is a bleak, bleak day for the English game.
Say it Ain't So, Pep. Say that none of this is true. Because, one of the greatest sadnesses of all in these guilty verdicts is that they tarnish the achievements in this country of Pep Guardiola , one of the greatest coaches that has ever lived. They tarnish everything that City have achieved since they were taken over by Abu Dhabi. They have brought the whole edifice crumbling down.
But it is not the greatest sadness. The greatest sadness is in the cost to fans of so many other rival clubs who were cheated of what they should have won. City's dishonesty robbed them of moments that would have lasted a lifetime. It robbed them of celebrations with friends that they would never have forgotten. It robbed them of days out that would have been forever bathed in sunshine.
Sir Alex Ferguson would have won 14 league titles, not 13, if City had not evaded the rules. Steven Gerrard 's domestic career with Liverpool would not have been defined by that slip against Chelsea in 2013-14 because Liverpool would have won the title. Manchester United would not still be wandering in a post-Ferguson wasteland because they would have won the title in 2017-18 under Jose Mourinho .
Pep Guardiola and Man City club chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak celebrate their 2024 title
Jurgen Klopp's Liverpool were among those beaten by City in the wake of their dishonesty
And Liverpool, not City, would have won one of the greatest title races of all time in 2018-19. And Jurgen Klopp and not Guardiola would have emerged victorious in that battle and history may have come to regard him as the greatest manager of the era that followed Ferguson instead.
Klopp's Liverpool came second to City in both the 18-19 and 21-22 title races by a solitary point. When he was asked after his departure in 2024 about the possibility of City being stripped of those titles, Klopp said: 'If you organise a bus parade, I am in. How long it takes I don't care.' That day may be coming sooner than he thought.
So the heartbreak lies in what others have lost as much as in the iniquity of what City gained. It lies in the defrauding of history and the way we were manipulated. City were a magnificent team to watch under Guardiola. Perhaps the best our league has ever seen. But that doesn't count for much anymore. Our eyes might as well have been scratched out. Our memories mean nothing now.
Some will say it is a great victory for the Premier League and, yes, it has established its authority over its member clubs and, yes, the alternative to winning this legal battle was unthinkable for it.
But the 'triumph' should make it question its direction of travel. This is a win for the Premier League in one way but in another, it is a catastrophic loss. City, and Guardiola, were its standard-bearers. They were its best team. They set new standards for beauty and quality. Now, it turns out, that was all built on sand. It may be that the league has won a battle but lost a wider war. City are part of the Premier League, too. The league is eating its own.
Everything that City have won since the Abu Dhabi takeover is discredited. Everything feels sullied. All the titles and trophies that were won between 2009 and 2018 are most at risk. The 'Aguerooo' moment from 2012 when City won their first top flight title for 44 years with a last-gasp winner from Sergio Aguero at the Etihad? That is tainted. That is spoiled. That is undermined.
The 'Aguerooo' moment from 2012 when City won their first top flight title is tainted
Jose Mourinho and Manchester United missed out on titles at the hands of Man City
Martin Tyler's greatest moment of commentary has been muted. The greatest moment in Premier League history? Not any more, it isn't. It may, in fact, come to be seen as a symbol of one of the most cursed eras in our national sport.
The guilty verdicts mean that City were playing by different rules to everybody else. And whatever you think of the rules, others respected them and so City should have done. The verdicts say they ignored the rules, that they manipulated the funds available to them unfairly. The verdicts say they had an unfair advantage. The verdicts say they cheated.
And so everything they achieved in those years is invalidated. And because those years provided the foundation upon which everything else was built, then everything that followed in the unparalleled success of the Pep Guardiola years is besmirched, too. No one is saying Guardiola knew what had passed before, of course, but he was an unwitting beneficiary of it.
And so what do we say now of the four top flight titles in a row that Guardiola's side won between 2020-21 and 2023-24? No other had done that in the long history of English football. That should have been Guardiola's greatest legacy but it turns out it was built on the shifting sands of the dishonesty of those that came before him. In a way, he too has been betrayed.
What now? Asterisks are not enough. The very least that should happen is that City be stripped of the titles they won in 2012, 2014, 2018, 2019, 2021, 2022, 2023, and 2024. That scenario is said to be 'unlikely'. It should not be. The very least that should happen is that they be relegated from the Premier League and made to start next season in the Championship.
They will appeal, of course, and so that will protect their participation in the Premier League for the rest of this season and perhaps beyond. But if that appeal is unsuccessful, they should be cast out of the top flight. The entire credibility of English football is at stake here. If they escape with a lesser punishment, credibility will be lost.
The unparalleled success of the Pep Guardiola years at Man City is besmirched, too
The guilty verdicts should also make English football pause and take a long, hard look at itself. The Premier League can celebrate its victory but it has become a place where owners have declared war on clubs' long-standing fans in their desire to maximise revenue and destroy tradition.
It should make the league look again at its willingness to allow nation-states to own its football clubs, as is currently the case with City and Newcastle United. The power that they wield and the fabulous riches they command and the arrogance that seeps from them led directly to the entire 115 charges farrago.
This may be just the beginning for City, too. It is a bleak day for them but it may get worse. The verdict could be a gateway for City's rivals each to claim more than £100million in compensation. I spoke to one high-ranking official at a rival Premier League club recently and he predicted an avalanche of law-suits against City if they were found guilty of the most serious charges.

articles.title_orig: White House blocks CNN from trip on Air Force One
articles.title_zh: White House blocks CNN from trip on Air Force One
articles.content_orig:
CNN had been scheduled to fly with Trump on Air Force One
US broadcaster CNN has been barred from travelling with President Donald Trump on Air Force One for a trip to Tennessee on Saturday.
The move is the latest in a battle between the White House and the media after it was forced to lift its ban on some news outlets.
CNN was scheduled to fly with Trump for his trip to Tennessee for a college American football game until a note released on Friday night by the White House did not list the broadcaster on the media schedule.
The BBC has requested comment from the White House.
CNN has reported that no other outlet was listed as replacing them in the president's tentative schedule.
Last week Trump banned CNN, Politico and MS NOW journalists from the White House after accusing them of writing "fiction or lies" about his administration.
All three media outlets said they were pursuing legal action , and accused Trump of violating their constitutional rights to free speech and freedom of the press.
Four television networks that have a daily rotation of White House coverage along with CNN - ABC, CBS, Fox News and NBC - had paused their broadcasts of the president in solidarity with the banned outlets.
The White House then launched its own streaming channel, Trump TV, ahead of the United General Assembly in New York.
A federal judge has since ruled Trump barring news outlets from the White House was likely unconstitutional and the administration had to let them back in, at least for now.
However, the White House still denied entry to some CNN and MS NOW reporters assigned to cover arrivals for a state dinner for Chinese leader Xi Jinping on Thursday.
A White House communications account earlier posted on X that "contrary to what the Fake News wants you to believe, they don't just get to have free rein into every part of the White House, every event, and every press call".
Regular US television coverage resumed on Friday after White House officials allowed reporters entry.
The president is set to attend a football game between University of Tennessee vs University of Texas College at Neyland Stadium in Knoxville from midday on Saturday.

articles.title_orig: Iran War Updates: Tehran proposes 7-day plan to reopen Strait of Hormuz as it seeks deal before U.S. midterms
articles.title_zh: Iran War Updates: Tehran proposes 7-day plan to reopen Strait of Hormuz as it seeks deal before U.S. midterms
articles.content_orig:
Iran’s seven-day timetable would restart nuclear talks, but will the US be willing to deliver on terms that include reining in Israel in Lebanon?
Iran’s seven-day timetable to reopen the strait of Hormuz and start talks on its nuclear programme has been pitched as a deal that could rapidly extricate Donald Trump from a political crisis but requires the US president to make difficult concessions.
In the five days left before the proposed reopening of the strait, which is expected to relieve pressure on global energy markets, Trump would need to lift Iranian asset freezes, permit Iran to export its oil and, probably most difficult of all, order Benjamin Netanyahu to end Israel’s attacks on Hezbollah in Lebanon , thus achieving the “ceasefire on all fronts”.
Iranian diplomats in New York said they thought a three-hour meeting earlier this week with the US envoy Steve Witkoff in which they laid out the seven-day plan was productive, but were doubtful the US would deliver.
Iran nevertheless feels it has done the diplomatic spadework, taking the proposal to China for endorsement and ensuring that Oman, located on the south side of the strait, was also on board.
The foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, explained that the idea was to take the elements of the Iran-US memorandum of understanding that Trump signed in June and repackage and accelerate the process since, as they understood it, Trump had come to hate the MoU.
“The conditions we have asked the US to meet is nothing new, nothing more than what was already in the Islamabad agreement, which was signed by the US president,” Araghchi said. But what is new is the speed.
In the first four to five days under this timetable, the US would have to lift the naval blockade on Iran’s oil ports, restore the waiver that lifted sanctions on Iran’s oil exports, end the war on all fronts and permit the release of some of Iran’s frozen assets.
On the sixth day, the strait of Hormuz would be reopened by Iran, with ships using a new route designated by Oman and Iran. And on the next day, negotiations would start on the future of Iran’s civil nuclear programme, including a protocol to allow UN nuclear inspectors back in to look at Iran’s damaged sites and the stockpile of highly enriched uranium. This accelerates the point at which nuclear talks would begin, from 60 days in the June agreement to seven.
Those talks could, of course, take a long time, but from Trump’s perspective, the strait of Hormuz would be reopened before the midterm elections, a point in the political calendar that the Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, says has never been a factor in Iranian thinking. Trump had claimed Iran was waiting until after the vote to offer a deal.
Iran, Araghchi argued at a largely off-the-record briefing with reporters – at which Pezeshkian was also present – had every reason not to negotiate with the US.
In particular, he admitted to being sceptical that Witkoff could deliver. He recounted how he had twice held talks with Trump’s special envoy, after which Witkoff had described them as “productive and good”, only for the US to bomb Iran the next day. Other Iranian diplomats say Trump’s willingness to rein in Netanyahu in Lebanon remains key. If he could do that, a deal would be feasible.
It is a difficult deal for Trump to swallow since the strait would reopen largely on Iran’s terms, with the new route predominantly going through Iranian waters. Saudi Arabia is also concerned that the route deal is bilateral between Iran and Oman, and not with the Gulf states as joint signatories.
Trump says he has a choice to make between the annihilation of Iran and engagement – an engagement that, he says with typical hyperbole, could make Iran one of the great countries of the world. In reality, the judgment he has to make is more prosaic. Is he prepared to go back to war with Iran after the midterms and, if not, does he believe the US can squeeze the Iranian economy so hard that the leadership will succumb.
Pezeshkian, who handed all questions about the talks to Araghchi, admitted Iranians wanted the war to end and did not deny the economic pressure, but said the public had withstood sanctions for 45 years.
He also insisted Iran’s decision-making machinery was functioning. The reclusive supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, was completely healthy, he claimed, a testimony based on spending seven hours in his presence. He did not explain why, apart from security, Khamenei had not issued a voice recording, photograph or video as proof of life.

articles.title_orig: Roads flood in New Jersey, inundate some homes, as first major signs of nor'easter take shape
articles.title_zh: Roads flood in New Jersey, inundate some homes, as first major signs of nor'easter take shape
articles.content_orig:
Surf breaks along the rocky coastline, with the twin lighthouses of Thatcher Island visible in the distance, during the early stages of a nor'easter Friday, Sept. 25, 2026, in Gloucester, Mass. Robert F. Bukaty/FR172387 AP Photo hide caption
Thousands were without power on the U.S. East Coast on Friday night as roads flooded in some coastal New Jersey communities, the first major signs of a powerful nor'easter expected to create dangerous conditions through the weekend.
Tens of millions of people are in the path of the storm already beginning to lash the region with strong winds and rain as it braces for much more. Dangerous flooding is expected along the Mid-Atlantic coast, particularly near New Jersey and Delaware, according to the National Weather Service.
In the coastal New Jersey borough of Surf City, water, with waves rippling along its surface, flooded the streets, inundating some homes. About 34 miles (54.7 kilometers) up the coast in the borough of Manasquan, where some roads were also flooding, Mayor Mike Mangan said he expected "a lot of water in the streets for a long time." A voluntary evacuation had been issued earlier in some low-lying areas of the community.
Concerts were canceled, along with dozens of flights going into airports in Boston, Nantucket and Martha's Vineyard on Friday and Saturday. Several airlines were offering to waive some change or cancellation fees for some East Coast flights through the weekend.
Brian Kelly, the mayor of the tiny New Jersey beach community Sea Bright, said the borough is bracing for winds up to 50 mph (80 kph) and flooding that could reach up to 6 feet (1.8 meters) on some streets. Officials expect the flooding to start Saturday and worsen by midday.
"It's going to be worse than average. We do have probably one or two flooding events a year, sometimes more, sometimes less, but I think this one will be closer to an Irene-scale flooding event," Kelly said, referencing the 2011 storm that caused major flooding in the Northeast. "I hope I'm wrong, but that's my gut feeling."
Kelly hopes hundreds of residents living in low-lying areas will consider evacuating. He said the town will open its recreation center for evacuees.
Peak wind gusts could approach 60 to 65 mph (97 to 105 kph) on Cape Cod, Martha's Vineyard and Nantucket on Friday night and Saturday, compared with about 50 to 55 mph (80 to 89 kph) around Boston and 35 to 40 mph (56 to 64 kph) farther inland, according to Matthew Belk, a meteorologist with NWS in Norton, Massachusetts.
"It's definitely going to be a case of the closer to the coast you are, the more impacts from the storm you're likely to see," Belk said.
Belk said nor'easters are not unusual as New England moves into fall, but one concern this early in the season is that leaves remain on the trees, creating more wind resistance. That could increase the risk of downed limbs, which in turn can cause power outages and leave debris in roads, he said.
Along the Atlantic coasts of New Jersey and Delaware, wind gusts could reach 60 mph (96.6 kph), according to NWS. In southeastern Connecticut and eastern Long Island, New York, gusts could get almost as high, potentially downing tree limbs and power lines.
More than 200 flights to and from airports in Boston, Nantucket, Martha's Vineyard and New York had been canceled Friday, and more cancellations were already in place for Saturday.
Meanwhile, the Red Sox announced their weekend series against the Chicago Cubs would be adjusted. The team moved the Sunday afternoon game to Friday to create a split doubleheader. Separately, Ed Sheeran announced that his high-profile Friday and Saturday shows at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts, would be canceled due to the storm.
The public ferry service connecting Cape Cod with the islands of Nantucket and Martha's Vineyard was experiencing widespread cancellations Friday due to strong winds and choppy water.
In Rhode Island, ferries were also canceled for Block Island. The disrupted ferry service was expected to also spill into Saturday.
For people who regularly travel to and from the islands, the possibility of getting stuck on one side or the other is "part of life," said Sean Driscoll, a spokesperson for the Woods Hole, Martha's Vineyard and Nantucket Steamship Authority. Most people have backup plans in place for when boats are canceled.
"It's a nuisance, but you know, we know what to do with this kind of stuff at this point," he said. "This is not out of the realm of ordinary."
Ashley Destino of Gloucester, a coastal city in northern Massachusetts, enjoyed a stroll along the beach with her two young children before preparing to hunker down at home during the storm.
"We came to the beach on Friday afternoon because we knew we were going to be inside all weekend," said Destino, who has Legos and arts and crafts activities prepared to entertain her two children, ages 7 and 4.
She also prepared by securing her boat with additional lines, and her husband pulled out a generator in case the electricity goes out.

articles.title_orig: TikTok to pay Alabama $100m and limit teenage use in first state settlement
articles.title_zh: TikTok to pay Alabama $100m and limit teenage use in first state settlement
articles.content_orig:
Trial had been set for Monday over claims by Alabama that TikTok misled parents about tools meant to shield children from harmful content
TikTok has agreed to pay Alabama at least $100m and enact time limits and other restrictions for teenage users, avoiding a trial with a settlement that was modelled on Instagram-owner Meta’s recent agreement with US states.
Alabama described it as a “first-in-the-nation settlement” with a state in the sweeping litigation over social media’s affect on teen wellbeing.
A trial had been set to begin on Monday in the southern US state over claims by Alabama that TikTok misled parents about tools meant to shield children from harmful content.
TikTok’s settlement with Alabama mirrors safety provisions agreed by Meta, including a two-hour daily time limit for teens, restricted access from midnight to 6am, and suspending notifications during school hours.
It will also strengthen age verification, ban beauty filters for teenagers, and offer young users a non-personalised content feed.
Attorney general Steve Marshall hailed Friday’s settlement as “a great day for Alabama parents”. He said: “Tonight, they can rest easier knowing real protections are in place to shield their children from the dangers of social media addiction.”
Under the settlement, TikTok will send $100m to Alabama and could possibly pay up to $300m in total if 40 other attorneys general sign similar agreements with the company within a specified timeframe.
Alabama’s suit was the latest in a wave of litigation targeting social media companies across the United States about alleged harm their apps cause young users.
In August, Meta agreed to pay $18bn to settle a sweeping lawsuit brought by US states accusing it of designing Instagram and Facebook to get children addicted.
In addition, the Alabama deal includes a conditional restriction that Meta also agreed to: expanding the night-time shutdown period to 10pm to 7am if other platforms also commit to do the same.
“TikTok’s priority has always been fostering a safe and positive space where people can be creative, discover what they love, and connect with their community,” a company spokesperson told AFP.
“This builds on our commitment and core objective to continually enhance our robust safety tools to protect teens,” the spokesperson added.
More than a dozen other states, including California and New York, still havesuits against TikTok.
The company has previously settled cases against it that were headed for trial, including a Los Angeles lawsuit brought by a young woman and a suit from a Kentucky school district.
Meta, by contrast, has taken its chances in court – with bruising results.
In March, a jury in New Mexico ordered the Facebook and Instagram owner to pay $375m after finding it had misled the public about the safety of its platforms for children.
That same month, a Los Angeles jury found Meta and Google’s YouTube negligent in the case of a 20-year-old woman who said she became hooked on social media as a child, awarding her $6m.
Going to trial would have exposed TikTok to unprecedented public scrutiny of how it handles safety, with company documents and executive testimony potentially aired in open court.
Alabama originally sued TikTok and its Chinese parent company ByteDance in April 2025, alleging the app was engineered to hook young users “just like a sophisticated gambling machine”.
The state later narrowed its case to claims under Alabama’s Deceptive Trade Practices Act, focusing on whether TikTok misrepresented the effectiveness of features such as “Restricted Mode” and “Kids Mode.”
The lawsuit accused TikTok of falsely claiming it limits access to sexual and violent content for young users to have its app rated safe for teens in app stores run by Google, Apple and Microsoft and of misleading users about the Chinese government’s access ‌to US users’ data.
TikTok said it designed its platform with teen safety as a key priority and argued that section 230 of the federal Communications Decency Act shields online platforms from liability for user-generated content.
With Agence France-Presse and Reuters

articles.title_orig: All the Major Social Media Networks Are Reportedly Refusing Ads for ‘Musk’
articles.title_zh: All the Major Social Media Networks Are Reportedly Refusing Ads for ‘Musk’
articles.content_orig:
Senior Editor, Technology and Politics
So much for free speech. The studio releasing Alex Gibney ’s new Elon Musk documentary Musk is finding itself unable to buy an ad on the biggest social platforms. YouTube , TikTok , and Instagram and Facebook owner Meta are all declining to run the trailer for Musk , along with X itself, The Hollywood Reporter has learned. That last one is perhaps understandable, given its owner. But the rejection by the other platforms has taken distributor Bleecker Street by surprise, and it is internally scrambling to understand why the ad has been rejected, according to a person familiar with the company’s processes who is not authorized to talk about them publicly. The unwillingness of platforms to accept even paid advertising is sure to raise concerns about free speech and the dwindling number of companies that control many of the platforms in this country — and ironically provide a proof-text for the very point the film is coming to make. Gibney’s doc is a four-hour look at a title character who attempts to control the conversation in various ways , including with alleged suppressions on X, which he bought in 2022.
Bleecker Street opens Musk in theaters on Oct. 9. YouTube, TikTok and Meta have all supplied a reason related to “political content” to Bleecker Street reps. The latter two companies’ platforms, by policy, do not allow campaign or other political ads, in Meta’s case largely owing to fallout from the Cambridge Analytica Facebook scandal during the 2016 election. But the Musk trailer, which dropped Thursday, does not appear to fall in the category of the campaign advertising those bylaws were enacted to prevent. It simply contains a shot of a political rally in 2024 and a reference at the end to the 2024 election — the kind of flicks that occur in numerous documentaries and are hardly meant to stump for a particular candidate in an upcoming race.
The reason for YouTube’s rejection is even less clear, as the platform does allow campaign ads, albeit with “paid for” disclosures from vetted candidates.
Bleecker Street has entered an appeal with all three companies. Meta has already rejected the appeal. TikTok and YouTube are still entertaining the petitions. For its part, X has refused to engage with Bleecker Street on the film or even accept advertising for any of its other films on its upcoming calendar. Press reps at Meta, TikTok, YouTube and X did not immediately provide a comment. A Bleecker Street representative confirmed that the ads were initially rejected but said they are continuing to appeal with all three companies besides X in the hope minds can be changed.
Traction on social media is key for a documentary release, which relies on word-of-mouth in a way a big-budget feature doesn’t.
The news also hits a nerve after Universal, which is releasing the film overseas, considered backing away from distributing Musk before capitulating to public pressure and commenting that it is standing by the film (though no details have yet been given).
It is unclear if there has been any communication between ad reps at X and the other social giants. Some other tech firms will also see their leaders under the Hollywood spotlight this fall, with Sony releasing Aaron Sorkin’s Mark Zuckerberg drama The Social Reckoning next month. That film’s trailer is currently available on YouTube.

articles.title_orig: Rogue OpenAI agents accessed US government websites
articles.title_zh: Rogue OpenAI agents accessed US government websites
articles.content_orig:
OpenAI has acknowledged that it alerted "dozens" of global institutions that their websites may have been meddled with by its AI bots acting improperly.
AI agents attempted to get information from "governments, universities, public agencies, and other institutions", including the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), Census Bureau and Education Department, the company said.
The disclosures come days after Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese announced that OpenAI agents had breached non-public files on the website of its government-run health care scheme.
Since August, public fears have grown over the potentially serious, even life-threatening, impacts of AI tools falling outside of human control.
OpenAI said that some of the data was accessed by AI agents, essentially bots that are designed and trained to operate somewhat autonomously, which were working to find "authoritative sources of public information".
But the company noted that some of the bots went beyond that and worked to bypass security measures on websites.
When attempting to get information from the Census Bureau, for instance, AI agents used tools reserved for software developers to access it, the company said.
OpenAI said all of the government data accessed by bots was public.
However, it noted that information that its bots accessed from the SEC, which regulates the US stock market and protects investors, was later published by AI agents on another website. OpenAI says this action was not intended.
In other instances that OpenAI disclosed on Friday, its AI agents transferred data when it should not have.
Such activity resulted in at least 53 incidents where an OpenAI agent took an image from ChatGPT user activity and transferred it elsewhere.
The company said that in each instance of a user image being used and transferred by an AI agent, the user had opted in to allow OpenAI to train models using their data.
Nevertheless, OpenAI admitted: "This is not an appropriate use of this data."
It added that the leak of user images occurred before it had put in place new safeguards on AI training, and it was working to get all the user images transferred to any third-party removed.
Reuters first reported the expanded investigations. OpenAI also published details to its public blog.
In certain instances of the agent activity, OpenAI said the tools "bypassed" security controls of some websites.
In other instances, the AI agents showed "misalignment" in attempts to get at information from websites. Misalignment is a term used by AI companies and researchers to describe instances where an AI tool did something that it was not trained to do or was otherwise unintended.
OpenAI said that it was limiting identifying what entities were impacted because many had asked the company to not disclose details.
"Our goal is to give each organization the facts and defer to them on if and when to make the incident public," it said.
Not all of the instances involved in this incident were being considered a significant security breach, the company noted.
"Some organizations may review what we share and conclude that the information was intentionally public or that the model's interaction was not concerning," it explained. "Others may identify a design issue or security weakness they want to address."
The company said many of the incidents are being referred to as "agent spam", which it described as "unexpected or concerning" AI agent activity, like posting information to the internet.
OpenAI began taking such incidents more seriously after an incident in July where a group, or "swarm," of its AI agents hacked the AI developer platform Hugging Face without being prompted to do so.
Hugging Face was first to go public with the incident, with OpenAI publicly taking responsibility for it later.
Clement Delangue, the head of Hugging Face, during a United Nations Security Council session on AI on Wednesday: "I often wonder what would have happened had I decided not to disclose this attack publicly."
"Especially now that we know similar incidents had been happening months earlier in secret at a handful of frontier labs without monitoring," Delangue added.
During that same UN meeting, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Dario Amodei, the head of rival firm Anthropic, asked for international leaders to form global standards for AI safety and ways to monitor and report such incidents.
While OpenAI and Anthropic have both said in recent weeks that they will bring third-party evaluators inside their companies to do real-time safety evaluations of AI tools and models, such evaluators have not yet arrived, as the BBC has reported .
OpenAI said on Friday that it is currently reviewing training activity by its AI agents and going back on a "month by month" basis from when the Hugging Face hack occurred.
"Most cases identified so far have been low severity, with limited or no evidence of meaningful impact," the company said. "Given the scale of the review required, and the need to verify each case, this work will take months to complete."
David Krueger, a professor of machine learning at University of Montreal and the founder of AI safety group Evitable, said on Friday that he was "deeply troubled" by the increasing number of AI-related safety incidents.
He called for "an immediate, indefinite, international moratorium" on AI development.
"We have yet to understand the extent of existing incidents, and future rogue AI scenarios could be catastrophic," Krueger said.

If there was one thing that was obvious from Meta Connect this year, it’s that the social media giant is all-in on its burgeoning line of smart glasses.
Indeed, the glasses were pretty much everywhere at the annual event, where Meta shows off its newest hardware and AI products. Both Meta staff and the flocks of influencers who frequent the event seemed to arrive with the glasses glued to their faces. Most of the demos the company offered this week also involved the glasses.
I swiftly joined the bespectacled masses and found myself trying on pair after pair of Meta’s high-tech specs.
One of the more notable products I had an opportunity to demo were Meta’s new, still-unreleased, audio-only smart glasses . News of these glasses emerged not long after the company weathered accusations that it was selling “pervert glasses,” with critics alleging that its camera-equipped specs could be used for nefarious surveillance purposes.
The new glasses come equipped with six microphones, but no camera, and they have no native way to record your surroundings, which should go a long way toward easing privacy concerns. They are significantly lighter than any of the other smart glasses I’ve worn, and they were quite comfortable.
The Meta staffer I talked to emphasized the glasses’ entertainment and communication options: You can listen to music easily (they’re more comfortable than earbuds) and take phone calls without reaching for your phone.
The glasses will also integrate with Muse, Meta’s personal agentic system, which can carry out tasks on the user’s behalf. The new integration, which isn’t yet available to the public, lets wearers speak to Muse and give it commands verbally. Meta also plans to personalize the agent, letting users pick from an assortment of cute digital avatars that can represent the agent when it communicates with them.
I was given an opportunity to try this out, which was fun but also somewhat comical. You have to be very direct with the agent, and you can’t talk to anyone else at the same time or it will get confused. Problematically, I kept chatting intermittently with the Meta staffer who’d given me the glasses, and the agent kept thinking I was speaking to it, so it would talk over her.
Still, in the right context, it’s easy to see how this new integration could be incredibly useful. If you don’t mind being seen in public talking to your own sunglasses, you’ll be able to ask Muse to take care of various digital tasks for you, like sending emails or reciting to-do lists, and it will handle them while you’re out grocery shopping or having a beer. You can also ask the glasses anything, and like a mobile version of ChatGPT, they’ll spit out an answer. (I asked the glasses a question about World War II, and they gave me a succinct and historically accurate response.)
Finally, I also got to test-drive a second audio-only pair: Meta’s new glasses for the hearing impaired. Given that hearing loss affects many families (some 50 million Americans are said to have some level of hearing loss), this device, unlike a lot of other modern tech gadgets, serves a clear and practical purpose.
I spoke briefly with a member of Meta’s research team who said the glasses had been in development for about five years, and he pointed out a price difference that could make them appealing: Whereas a lot of hearing aids can run as high as $1,600, the glasses will sell for $150.
The experience of wearing these glasses was interesting. Meta had me put earplugs in before trying them on to simulate the hearing loss that the glasses are meant to help users overcome. Once the glasses were on, they seemed to amplify the voice of the person I was talking to. Users can switch the amplification from focused, which zeroes in on the person in front of them, to omnidirectional, which picks up sound from all around them, depending on how they want to experience their surroundings.
Mark Zuckerberg has made it clear that he believes smart glasses are the future, and it’s evident that his company is doing its best to fulfill that vision. But smart glasses remain a niche that has yet to truly find its footing. What was most obvious at Connect is that Meta has — in an attempt to succeed where others have failed — cast a very wide net, trying to make its glasses stylish, functional, and, most of all, useful.
Is this the future? Unsurprisingly, everyone at Connect seemed to think so. I suppose we’ll have to see if the rest of the world follows suit.

articles.title_orig: Trump cancels nearly $1bn in funding approved by Congress
articles.title_zh: Trump cancels nearly $1bn in funding approved by Congress
articles.content_orig:
President using rare power to revoke expenditure with bipartisan approval to aid immigrant services
Donald Trump is canceling nearly $1bn in spending approved by Congress, the White House announced on Friday, using a rare and contested power to axe funding for immigrant services and diversity-focused initiatives.
Trump’s office of management and budget described the funding cut as focused on “the most harmful government spending”.
Most of the cuts are focused on services for immigrants, including non-profits that serve refugees and unaccompanied minors accused of being in the country illegally. The administration says the funds are no longer necessary because illegal border crossings have diminished considerably.
A White House press release announcing the funding rescissions notes that some of the organizations are led by people who worked in the administration of Democratic president Barack Obama.
Trump’s move was condemned by senator Susan Collins, a Republican in a tough re-election campaign and chair of the Senate appropriations committee.
Collins said in a statement the action came without warning or consultation. She also said she would work to address with colleagues “these illegal actions”.
“Not only is the delay itself an impoundment that was not reported to Congress, but also it is a usurpation of Congress’s appropriations powers,” Collins said. “OMB is an agency of the executive branch. It does not get to decide which programs are worth funding.”
“This is theft from the American people, plain and simple,” Patty Murray, the Washington Democratic senator, who is vice-chair of the appropriations committee said in a statement . “These are funds Congress has delivered on a bipartisan basis and should be helping people – not cut off by a president more focused on building a ballroom than investing in families. Every Republican who voted for these bills should be furious, because [Russell] Vought is saying their votes don’t count.”
Typically, Congress can review the president’s proposed spending cuts before they take effect. But Trump made that all but impossible by announcing them with just five days left in the federal fiscal year. The government accountability office has called the maneuver , known as a “pocket rescission,” illegal.
Collins called it the latest attempt by OMB to “undermine Congress’s constitutional power of the purse”.
A year ago, Trump issued a pocket rescission for the first time in 50 years by blocking $4.9bn in congressionally approved foreign aid. The US supreme court declined to block those rescissions, saying that Trump’s authority over foreign affairs weighed heavily in its decision. This year, Trump is targeting domestic spending.
The use of a pocket rescission fits part of a broader pattern by the Trump administration to exact greater control over the US government, eroding the power of Congress.
The administration has also fired federal workers, imposed a historic increase in tariffs, and started the war in Iran without going through Congress, putting the burden on the judicial branch to determine the limits of presidential power.

articles.title_orig: Trump said he would campaign in midterm battlegrounds. He's starting in deep red states instead
articles.title_zh: Trump said he would campaign in midterm battlegrounds. He's starting in deep red states instead
articles.content_orig:
Donald Trump seems to be playing defense with his choice of midterm campaign stops in the coming weeks. He’ll soon travel to states where Republicans are suddenly having to defend Senate seats.
Next month, the 80-year-old president will travel to four states where Republicans are supposed to be safe but are suddenly facing competitive Senate races: Texas, Alaska, Iowa, and Florida.
In Texas, where a Democrat hasn’t won a statewide office in over three decades, James Talarico leads Trump-endorsed Attorney General Ken Paxton, 50 percent to 44 percent, according to a Marist poll released this week.
In Alaska, Democrat Mary Peltola leads incumbent Dan Sullivan by four and five points, according to two polls released two weeks ago.
Iowa Senate candidate Josh Turek, who has Barack Obama’s coveted endorsement, leads Ashley Hinson by eight points in a Marist poll conducted last week.
In Florida, Trump’s home state, polls have favored the GOP, whose Senate and gubernatorial candidates held double-digit leads in a Stetson University survey this week.
Next week, Trump will make very different kinds of stops in deep-red states that have not been a focus of concerned Republicans’ efforts to maintain their slim majorities in Congress. He will appear in Durant, Oklahoma, next Thursday, the Republican National Committee announced . The next day he will stop in Mobile, Alabama, Politico reported . The Trump 47 Committee, the president’s joint fundraiser with the RNC, is hosting each event.
Each state widely backed Trump in the last three presidential elections, meaning the president is sure to revel in past victories. But the utility of stopping there ahead of the midterms is questionable, given how few—if any—races of importance are competitive. Those stops look more like emotional support rallies than attempts to shore up vulnerable Republican candidates.
Each state’s Senate contest is rated “solid” Republican by the Cook Political Report. So are the gubernatorial races . Of the combined 12 House contests in both states, 10 are considered “solid” Republican, and one “solid” Democrat. The outlier is in Alabama’s second congressional district, which the GOP state legislature redrew to carry out Trump’s redistricting effort. The seat, currently held by a Democrat, is now considered “likely” to turn red.
Beginning Oct. 3, Trump will make stops in other “traditional” battleground states, a source told Politico.
The White House referred questions about the president’s schedule to the RNC, which did not immediately respond to the Daily Beast.
Spokesperson Natalie Baldassarre told Politico: “While Democrats squabble over the last two cents their party has to spare, the president is barnstorming the country, energizing our base, and supercharging Republican candidates in key races and beyond. We have the resources to spend, and Republicans are full steam ahead to protect and expand our majorities.”
With early voting already underway in some states, and amid a flurry of troubling polls on affordability and the Iran war, Republicans have been forced to spend on races that had once been seen as theirs to win. A leaked memo from the Senate GOP’s campaign arm is urging donors to open their wallets for candidates in Alaska, Iowa, and Ohio, where former Sen. Sherrod Brown leads by four points, according to RealClearPolitics’ polling average
Meanwhile, Republicans have all but conceded two Senate seats they had hoped to win not long ago: Georgia and North Carolina.

articles.title_orig: Ethiopia fighting: Are Tigray's TPLF forces and the army heading back to war?
articles.title_zh: Ethiopia fighting: Are Tigray's TPLF forces and the army heading back to war?
articles.content_orig:
Fighting has erupted in Ethiopia's northern region of Tigray between regional forces and the national army.
Tigray residents, who have been trying to recover from a brutal two-year war that ended in 2022, fear a return to full-scale conflict.
There are reports of panic buying - and now internet and call services have been disrupted.
This means people cannot get access to their money via digital apps in what has become a largely cashless society after ATMs stopped working several months ago.
It follows more than six months of worsening relations between the government and the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), the party that runs Tigray.
The African Union (AU) brokered a peace deal, known as the Pretoria Agreement, between the two sides, ending the war nearly four years ago - but several issues have remained unresolved that have inflamed tensions.
This year, both sides have been trading blame while troops have mobilised amid pockets of fighting.
This week, major clashes erupted in Tigray and quickly spread into the neighbouring Afar and Amhara regions. The two sides disagree over who started the latest escalation.
The TPLF says it was responding to a federal offensive, including drone strikes, while the government says Tigrayan forces attacked first after seizing control of airports in Tigray.
For much of Tigray's modern political history, it has been governed by the TPLF, which first emerged as an armed movement in the 1970s fighting Ethiopia's military government.
It became a major force in the overthrow of the Marxist regime in 1991 and went on to become the most powerful component of the Ethiopian People's Revolutionary Democratic Front (EPRDF), the coalition that governed the ethnically diverse country for nearly three decades.
At times this proved contentious as some felt the TPLF held too much sway as Tigrayans only make up around 6% of Ethiopia's population.
When Abiy Ahmed became prime minister in 2018, he replaced the EPRDF with the Prosperity Party, significantly watering down the TPLF's influence.
Relations between Addis Ababa and the TPLF rapidly deteriorated until war erupted in 2020 in what was one of the most deadly conflicts this century.
The AU mediator estimated some 600,000 people died during the war, which totally cut off Tigray from the outside world and drove the region to the precipice of famine.
An uneasy truce was agreed in November 2022.
There are four key issues - and two concern the fertile area of western Tigray.
The TPLF lost control of this territory in the early days of the war to Amhara, a region which neighbours Tigray to the west and whose fighters had fought on the side of the Ethiopian army.
Many people in Amhara believe the territory of western Tigray should never have been incorporated into Tigray when regional boundaries were redrawn after the military regime was ousted in 1991.
When its fighters seized control during the recent civil war, hundreds of thousands of ethnic Tigrayan people fled and are now living in homeless camps in Tigray and in the capital, Addis Ababa.
The TPLF wants western Tigray back and for those displaced from the territory to return. The government says the future of the territory needs to be decided by a referendum.
For the government, a major matter of contention has been disarmament. It says the TPLF has only handed over old weaponry to the AU and has been hiding its arms.
The two sides have also been at loggerheads over how Tigray should be governed. Under the terms of the deal, an interim administration was appointed by Abiy.
But attempts by the prime minister to influence affairs caused disputes within the TPLF itself and just before the general election in May, which was not held in Tigray because of the security situation, it restored its pre-war administration, disbanding the one set up by Abiy.
This has meant that civil servants are longer being paid and other services have been seizing up, worsening economic conditions.
A major development has seen the TPLF, once politically isolated inside Ethiopia, gain several key allies.
Earlier in September, it joined six other armed movements in forming what is called the Alliance for Survival, which includes those actively fighting the government like Amhara's Fano militia and the Oromo Liberation Army.
Members of the new alliance have different grievances, but they do share one  objective: they want to remove Abiy's government from power.
So while the TPLF and Fano forces were on opposite sides during the civil war - and still disagree over the fate of western Tigray - they have temporarily put some of their differences aside.
TPLF officials say they do not want to repeat the situation of 2020, when they felt surrounded and isolated.
Yet analysts caution the alliance may become difficult to maintain because its members ultimately have very different interests.
As well as blaming the TPLF for starting the recent fighting, it has criticised the new alliance, portraying it as an attempt to destabilise the country.
It has also accused Eritrea of supporting armed groups inside Ethiopia, something Asmara denies.
During the recent civil war, Eritrea fought alongside Ethiopian troops but the two neighbours, which have long had a volatile relationship, have again fallen out.
Their disagreement centres on the Red Sea and its ports.
Ethiopia, the world's most populous landlocked nation, lost access to them when Eritrea seceded in 1993. Recently Prime Minister Abiy has been pushing for ownership of Eritrea's southern port of Assab - about 60km (37 miles) from the border - and hinted at taking it by force.
Reports indicate that federal forces have been using drones and other military operations against Tigrayan forces.
The government's stated justification is that it is responding to attacks and trying to defend federal positions and territory. However, the circumstances surrounding individual strikes are difficult to independently verify.
Residents in one recently targeted town told the BBC the drones had hit two schools, which local officials said had been used by Ethiopian troops as military bases during the war.
This suggests Addis Ababa may believe they are again being used for a military purpose - by Tigrayan forces.
The attacks have come amid reports that the TPLF has been forcibly recruiting young men to join its ranks.
The main diplomatic effort is being led by the AU, which has called for an immediate cessation of hostilities and a return to direct talks.
It has asked former Nigerian President Olusegun Obasanjo, the AU's special Horn of Africa envoy, to engage the parties urgently.
The UN has made a similar appeal, warning against a wider and more devastating conflict.
The regional organisation Igad has also called for fighting to stop and dialogue to resume.
The difficulty is that trust between Addis Ababa and Tigray is extremely low, while the formation of the new armed alliance has made the situation more complicated.
Yes, there is a significant risk of wider conflict inside Ethiopia.
The fighting has already moved to areas over and along Tigray's borders, while the government is simultaneously dealing with armed conflicts in other regions, particularly Amhara and Oromia.
The new alliance potentially connects several of these conflicts politically and militarily.
There is also a fear that Eritrea could be drawn in again - this time against the government.
The two aggressors in Sudan's civil war are also on opposite sides when it comes to allegiances in Tigray, potentially complicating matters.
The AU has specifically urged all neighbouring countries not to take actions that could further escalate the crisis.

articles.title_orig: Pope Leo XIV warns AI could undermine humanity during France visit
articles.title_zh: Pope Leo XIV warns AI could undermine humanity during France visit
articles.content_orig:
Pope Leo XIV has warned that artificial intelligence, which he referred to as a “paradise of machines”, and other emerging technologies could undermine humanity by posing fundamental questions about what it means to be human.
Thousands gathered to welcome the pope in France on Friday, shortly after he raised existential questions about technological advancement and human rights during his opening speech to President Emmanuel Macron and authorities at the Elysee Palace and then to diplomats and United Nations employees at the headquarters of UNESCO, the UN culture and education organisation.
“If we are to avoid losing our humanity amid a paradise of machines invading and conditioning our daily lives, there is an urgent need for education in ethical discernment,” Pope Leo said beside Macron.
Scientific progress should not turn “into profit-driven ventures promoting genetic manipulation, surrogacy, the trade in human organs or the possibility of arranging one’s own death”, the pope said, a few months after France passed a landmark bill legalising assisted dying.
He reaffirmed the Vatican’s opposition to nuclear weapons, stating that the nuclear deterrence doctrine was “mistaken” as it was heightening a new arms race.
The pope identified AI as one of the greatest challenges currently facing humanity since the very beginning of his pontificate, dedicating his first encyclical to the topic to call for significant regulation and for developers to work for the common good.
“The paradox has become increasingly evident: while ‘intelligence’ is attributed to computational systems, we struggle to recognise the inalienable dignity of human persons, whose lives are judged according to the criterion of efficiency and, when deemed no longer productive, are rejected and discarded,” he said.
The pope had earlier told reporters that he was pleased that his message was being heard by AI developers and hoped the dialogue would continue between tech companies and the Vatican.
“And I think from their perspective, many of them, they’re very much open to looking for ways of making sure that AI does not displace or ultimately destroy humanity, but rather is a tool for human beings,” he said.
The pope’s four-day trip marks the first official papal visit to France in 18 years. While secularism is enshrined in the country’s constitution, the pontiff stressed that “authentic secularity” should not exclude religion “from the public sphere or from education”.
Thousands of worshippers cheered Leo on Friday as he stepped up to pray and called those gathered at a stadium near Paris the “saints of France”. Earlier in the afternoon, the pope crossed central Paris in his popemobile.
The Vatican estimated that about 300,000 people had come out to see the pontiff on Friday.

articles.title_orig: What the Supreme Court's voter-citizenship database decision means for the midterms
articles.title_zh: What the Supreme Court's voter-citizenship database decision means for the midterms
articles.content_orig:
A version of this story appeared in CNN’s What Matters newsletter. To get it in your inbox, sign up for free here .
Election Day is fast approaching, but the Supreme Court is still weighing in on the rules — most recently on Friday when it allowed states to use a Trump administration - backed tool to ferret out noncitizen voting there’s little evidence occurs in a widespread way.
Nobody wants noncitizens voting illegally, but the move by justices less than two months from Election Day raises the real concern that legal citizen voters could find themselves unable to cast ballots.
Supreme Court justices have already been faced with multiple questions about the coming election.
They gutted the Voting Rights Act , supercharging a race to redraw congressional maps this year and into the future.
One state, Missouri , was still wondering Friday which congressional districts its voters would cast ballots in come November because lower courts weighed in after the high court. Never mind that ballots had already been printed and mailed.
An unsigned Friday evening decision from the Supreme Court — which sided with opponents of the proposed districts for the third time in as many weeks — seemed likely to put to rest a whirlwind legal saga that bounced through state and federal courts for much of September. Republican Gov. Mike Kehoe said Friday that Missouri would follow the court’s order.
While the justices in other cases blessed the redrawing of maps for partisan gain, they hit pause, at least for now, on the Trump administration’s plan to upend mail-in voting writ large, tabling that issue for the next election.
Noncitizen voting has been a bugbear for Trump for years. He has alleged there is widespread fraud even in elections he won, although neither of his administrations has been able to find much evidence.
I asked CNN’s Fredreka Schouten, a national political writer, about the database this decision unleashes and what it could mean for people trying to cast ballots.
SCHOUTEN: It’s a federal tool known as the Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements. It’s been around for decades and has long been used to verify the citizenship and immigration status of people seeking government benefits. And some election officials have had agreements in the past to use the tool, for a fee, to check the citizenship status of voters.
But the Trump administration dramatically revamped it, starting last year. It’s now linked to lots of government data as part of the administration’s push to hunt for potential noncitizens on the voting rolls.
SCHOUTEN: The SAVE America Act is different but sort of related in that they are both focused on the question of whether only US citizens are casting ballots.
The SAVE America Act would have dramatically revamped voting rules across the country, requiring voter ID to cast a ballot and mandating that people provide documents, such as a birth certificate of US passport, proving their citizenship when they register to vote. It would also put pressure on states to use the SAVE data system and other data tools like it for purging rolls.
Critics say many legitimate voters don’t have easy access to those documents and argue the proposal would have disenfranchised many Americans.
I should say here that experts note that voting by noncitizens in federal elections, which is already illegal, is exceedingly rare. But this has become an animating issue for the president.
SCHOUTEN: The Trump administration linked the information already in SAVE to other federal data, most notably Social Security Administration records, which cover most Americans.
The administration then encouraged election officials to carry out bulk uploads of their states’ registration rolls and waived any fee to do so. Tens of millions of records were run through the system before a federal judge blocked its use earlier this year.
With Friday’s ruling, the US Supreme Court has allowed SAVE to be used again for reviewing voter rolls.
SCHOUTEN: That’s not entirely clear.
The high court’s opinion emphasized that SAVE can be used for “individualized” checks of a voter’s citizenship in the upcoming election but also noted that federal law prohibits mass purges close to Election Day.
But the administration has argued that the federal ban on mass removals within 90 days of an election doesn’t apply to purges involving noncitizens who were improperly registered in the first place. The Supreme Court will decide that question in a case this coming term — but not before the midterms.
SCHOUTEN: Let’s back up a bit.
In addition to encouraging states to use SAVE to conduct their own reviews of their voting rolls, the Justice Department has been on a campaign to obtain each state’s full, unredacted lists of voters, including personal information about voters, such as full dates or birth and partial Social Security numbers, to do its own check on whether states are complying with federal law.
When those states refused, the DOJ sued. So far, the agency has lost all 25 cases in which a judge has ruled.
But federal agencies have moved forward with efforts to try to find potential noncitizens on voting rolls — including using publicly available voter lists. A recent whistleblower complaint released by several Democrats on Capitol Hill alleged that agents in the Department of Homeland Security, who were tasked with rooting out voter fraud, are being kept in the dark about the sources of some of the data being used in their reviews.
And the dispute the Supreme Court was ruling on Friday was the administration’s ability to offer the SAVE systems to states that want to voluntarily want to use it for their own voter list maintenance.
SCHOUTEN: One overarching worry from critics of the SAVE tool is that it’s not reliable.
Take Texas, for example. State officials there ran all 18 million names of its voters through the SAVE tool last year and announced that their audit had found 2,724 potential noncitizens and directed counties to give voters 30 days to verify their citizenship or be removed from the rolls.
Those numbers began dropping once local election officials began digging — in part, because the system doesn’t appear to properly track naturalized citizens.
Earlier this year, I interviewed a Texas resident who became ensnared by the audit. She was born in Argentina and was a naturalized US citizen, yet state officials tagged her as a suspected noncitizen. She was able to quickly send in a scan of her US passport and remain a voter.
Earlier this month, Texas officials announced that hundreds of potential noncitizens flagged last year were indeed Americans and eligible to vote and called on local officials to reinstate their registrations if they had been removed.
SCHOUTEN: If you are worried about this or any other voting issue, you can always verify your registration status with your local election office. There’s enough time before the general election to fix any problems.
CNN’s Tierney Sneed contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: 2026 WNBA playoffs: Biggest questions for Lynx-Liberty, Aces-Fever and every first-round series
articles.title_zh: 2026 WNBA playoffs: Biggest questions for Lynx-Liberty, Aces-Fever and every first-round series
articles.content_orig:
We've finally made it to Money Time, folks.
The WNBA playoffs will be tipping off this weekend, and we've been blessed with four dynamic matchups with varying degrees of star power, scheme versatility, and all the storylines you can hope for if #narratives are your portion.
For this year's preview, we'll be looking at a big picture question for each series, then sprinkling in some other thoughts and questions that may matter moving forward.
Lynx-Liberty • Dream-Mystics • Valkyries-Wings • Aces-Fever
Lynx (33-11): 3rd in offense, 4th in defense, 2nd in net rating
Liberty (26-18): 6th in offense, 7th in defense, 7th in net rating
Season series: Liberty 2-1
THE BIG QUESTION: Is Olivia Miles ready for playoff pressure?
Don't take this as your typical "rookie experiences her first playoff series" point. I don't doubt, assuming she's healthy enough ( please let the calf be OK), that Miles will be ready from a competitive standpoint.
I mean this more in a literal sense. One of the most fascinating trends in the league to me has been teams progressively picking up Miles higher on the court as the season has gone on. Per Second Spectrum, the pick-up points for Miles have increased every month:
That jump in September is notable, man. Look no further than the most recent matchup between the Lynx and Liberty, where the mixture of Leonie Fiebich , Pauline Astier and Rebekah Gardner took turns hounding Miles well beyond half-court. It's not that Miles is incapable of beating that type of aggression; she certainly has the speed, handle and elite blend of driving juice and playmaking gumption to beat it.
But that kind of ball pressure and length can just … weigh on you. Miles finished that game with 20 points, 8 rebounds and 5 assists – not bad, until you add in that she went 5-of-18 from the field and also turned the ball over five times.
(Also of note: Fiebich on Miles specifically is a cross-match worth monitoring. Assuming Breanna Stewart gets the Napheesa Collier matchup, the Liberty will be empowered to switch any Miles-Collier actions. Having to deal with the collective size of Fiebich and Jonquel Jones , if you want to get Natasha Howard involved as a screener, isn't fun either. During their regular season meetings, the Lynx generated only 0.8 points per possession on trips featuring a Miles-Howard pick-and-roll.)
The broader question of how well the Lynx will deal with physicality certainly looms large, but I think we'll get some early answers based on how successful Miles is dealing with it early in possessions.
You never want to be reductive when it comes to playoff time, but this series may very well be decided by whichever backcourt decides to show up. Beyond Miles, the Lynx will need a quality shotmaking and decision-making series from Courtney Williams . The Liberty are simply a different (and much better) team when Sabrina Ionescu comes to the party, and the mix of drives and defensive ball pressure from Astier will be key in this one.
The Liberty rebounded 31.6% of their own misses this season (5th). The Lynx once again ranked toward the bottom of the league in defensive rebound rate (67.7%, 11th). The paint itself will be an important battleground in this series, but the rebound battle will swing things.
Just to briefly circle back: sign me up for potentially three games of Stewie ( please let the knee be OK) and Phee. We're talking two of the, what, four best players in the league at full-tilt? I'm excited to watch them deal with each other. This is a match made in two-way versatility heaven.
Dream (30-14): 4th in offense, 3rd in defense, 3rd in net rating
Mystics (28-16): 12th in offense, 2nd in defense, 8th in net rating
Season series: Mystics 2-1
THE BIG QUESTION: Whose half-court offense can find daylight?
If you want off-ball hand-fighting, crowded (and dangerous) lanes, and rugged paint play, this is the series for you.
The young Mystics (I refuse) have earned their stripes behind a defense that doesn't let you breathe. Shakira Austin ( please be OK) and Sonia Citron headline this unit; Citron may have been the best wing defender in basketball, while Austin's blend of scheme versatility and rim protection made her a(nother) worthy Defensive Player of the Year candidate. Michaela Onyenwere is a fantastic defender in her own right (with All-Defense level metrics and tracking data to boot), while Kiki Iriafen has quietly grown into a quality defender that can hold her own in space.
On the other side, the Dream boast the likely frontrunner for Defensive Player of the Yea r in Angel Reese , a rangy thief in Rhyne Howard (who would probably be an All-Pro corner in another lifetime), a smaller-but-still-deadly thief in Jordin Canada , plus a pair of defenders in Allisha Gray and Naz Hillmon that can perform at an All-Defense level on any given night.
No team turns you over quite like the Dream; seriously, they forced turnovers on a league-high 19.5% of possessions. That doesn't seem to bode well for a Mystics group that turned the ball over on 19.2% of their possessions, the worst mark in the league.
No team mashes the paint quite like the Mystics, ranking first in the percentage of points that come in the paint, offensive rebound rate, and free throw rate. That doesn't seem to bode well for a Dream group that fouls quiiite a bit (11th in opponent free throw rate).
I've had questions about both of these half-court offenses throughout the year, so it's a bit funny (and fitting) that they have to face each other in the first round.
Tied to the overall paint battle, I wonder what the scoring approach for Howard and Gray will be. Gray's the more consistent downhill threat, and Howard's at her best when she can complement her perimeter shotmaking (44.8% on 9.7 3s against the Mystics this year) with some drives. The Mystics, more than anyone else, have made their lives difficult when they've tried to pressure the rim. Per Second Spectrum, the Mystics had at least one help defender present on 83% of drives from Howard or Gray. Their combined 0.91 PPP clip on drives against the Mystics was their worst against any opponent.
Actually, we'll stay in the paint a beat longer. How impactful will rookie centers Lauren Betts (Mystics) and Madina Okot (Dream) be in this series? With Bri Jones done for the season, Okot will be needed for some important spot minutes. Betts generally keeps the rim protection (and offensive rebounding) train rolling when she checks in for Austin or Iriafen; the Mystics will need that to maintain their paint edge.
Do not sleep on the offensive importance of Canada (she's made a lot of plays in clutch situations) and, on the Mystics' side, Georgia Amoore . Coach of the Year candidate Sydney Johnson has spoken about Amoore's importance as an organizer; if she's able to make enough shots, the Point Sonia lineups could feel like more of a bonus than a necessity.
Valkyries (32-12): 7th in offense, 1st in defense, 1st in net rating
Wings (27-17): 5th in offense, 6th in defense, 6th in net rating
Season series: Valkyries 3-0
THE BIG QUESTION: Can the Wings crack the code on Golden State's defense?
It's not enough to acknowledge the Valkyries having the league's stingiest defense (99.1 defensive rating). Their defense, per PBP Stats, was nearly 10 points better than league average — making it (statistically, at least) the stingiest defense of all time.
The Wings, headlined by the All-Star duo of Paige Bueckers and Jessica Shepard , posted a franchise-best 111.3 offensive rating during the regular season. They could only muster a 97.8 offensive rating across their three winless matchups against the Valkyries this season.
Having the trio of Veronica Burton , Gabby Williams and Kiah Stokes to throw at Bueckers, Arike Ogunbowale (a former All-Star in her own right) and Shepard is quite the luxury, and that's before mentioning the other high-wattage options (former Wings Kaila Charles and Kayla Thornton chief among them) they can and did cycle in.
